name: Wasmi
baseline: Wasmtime (Cranelift), Wasmer (Cranelift) and V8 for startup; WAMR fast interpreter and Wasmtime Pulley for execution
workload: wasmi-benchmarks startup suite: compile + instantiate of 7 modules from tiny (erc20) to huge (ffmpeg, spidermonkey), geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Startup geomean on AMD EPYC 7763, relative to the per-case fastest runtime (lower is better): Wasmi v2 (lazy) x1.37 and Wasmi v1 (lazy) x1.56, versus Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1634.19, Wasmer (Cranelift) x1484.15, Wasmtime (Winch) x298.15, Wasmer (Singlepass) x162.12 and V8 x33.27; about 1,190x lower than Wasmtime Cranelift (derived from page data). Eager Wasmi v2 is x38.88, still below both Cranelift runtimes.
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks Cargo.toml: [profile.bench] lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1; Rust toolchain version not pinned in the repo and the C/C++ runtimes are built by their Rust wrapper crates under that profile (not verified)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: Interpreter: steady-state execution is about 11x slower than Wasmtime Cranelift (x12.40 vs x1.15 on the execution geomean, derived from page data at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg). The fast startup depends on lazy compilation, and the 'lazy' modes defer validating function bodies until first call. Wasmi v2 was a beta (v2.0.0-beta.7) in the benchmark README.
caveats: The suite is maintained by the Wasmi authors, so it is third-party for every runtime except Wasmi. Ratios were read from the text labels of the rendered SVG (labels and values are both in descending order); the README gives no hardware itself. Startup ratios are dominated by modules where lazy compilation skips most functions; eager mode (x38.88) is a fairer compile-cost comparison. Execution geomean on the same CPU: Wasmi v2 (eager) x12.40 beats WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51 and Wasmtime (Pulley) x27.92, but loses to Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1.15 and V8 x1.05. Wasmi README itself shows no numbers.
found_via: WebSearch 'wasm runtimes benchmark shootout github wasmtime wasmer wazero wasmi wasm3 interpreter JIT AOT performance comparison repo' -> github.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks and its wasmi-benchmarks-plots repo

name: wasm3
baseline: Wasmtime Pulley interpreter and WAMR fast interpreter (execution); Wasmtime and Wasmer Cranelift (startup)
workload: Interpreter-only comparison of 7 runtimes on Apple Silicon E-cores: 17 shared cases (call_indirect and vtable dispatch, xmrsplayer, sqlite3 speedtest1, graphql validation, audio DSP and others), CPU time per call.
claimed_speedup: CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime, geometric mean over 17 cases, N=10: Apple M4 Max E-cores wasm3 1.01, WAMR 1.63, Pulley 2.09 (wasm3 about 2.1x faster than Pulley and 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp, derived from page data); iPhone XS (A12) E-cores wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68.
compiler_and_flags: wasm3 v0.9.0: -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions, Apple clang 21.0.0; Pulley built with Rust nightly-2026-07-05, fat LTO, 1 CGU, --cfg=pulley_tail_calls; WAMR cmake Release -O3 with FAST_INTERP=1 and AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (E-cores via taskpolicy -b) and iPhone XS Max (Apple A12 Bionic, E-cores)
tradeoffs: Interpreter only. Of the Wasm 3.0 features the harness tests it has only tail calls and extended-const (no GC, typed references, exceptions, memory64). Instantiating the extended-const modules costs 62-122x Pulley's time. README says the project is in a minimal-maintenance phase.
caveats: Third-party harness, but it compares against a forked Wasmtime (v49.0.0 + 9 commits by the harness author) and a WAMR main build carrying 29 patches, on Apple Silicon only, and it excludes JIT/AOT tiers. On x86-64 the lead shrinks: wasmi-benchmarks on AMD EPYC 7763 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) has Wasm3 (eager) execution geomean x16.51 vs WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07 and Wasmtime (Pulley) x27.92, while Wasmtime (Cranelift) is x1.15; its startup geomean (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-startup.svg) has Wasm3 (lazy) x2.77 vs Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1634.19 (lazy compilation). Frank Denis's 2021 libsodium shootout (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks/HEAD/2021-Q1/README.md) also reports 'wamr was slower than wasm3 on every single test' and native about 30x faster than wasm3 (2021 numbers).
found_via: WebSearch 'github WebAssembly interpreter faster than wasm3 OR faster than wasmtime benchmark CoreMark C++ runtime' -> rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark; also wasmi-benchmarks and the jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2021-Q1 README

name: WebAssembly Micro Runtime (WAMR) fast interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison of 7 runtimes on Apple Silicon E-cores: 17 shared cases, CPU time per call (WAMR built with FAST_INTERP=1, AOT/JIT/FAST_JIT off).
claimed_speedup: CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime, geometric mean over 17 cases, N=10: Apple M4 Max E-cores WAMR 1.63 vs Pulley 2.09 (WAMR about 1.28x faster, derived from page data); iPhone XS (A12) E-cores WAMR 1.38 vs Pulley 1.68 (about 1.22x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cmake Release, -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12; INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0 SIMD=1 RELAXED_SIMD=1 and others, WAMR_DISABLE_HW_BOUND_CHECK=1; Pulley: Rust nightly-2026-07-05, fat LTO, --cfg=pulley_tail_calls; Apple clang 21.0.0
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (E-cores) and iPhone XS Max (Apple A12 Bionic, E-cores)
tradeoffs: The shipped fast interpreter has no GC, typed references, memory64, multi-memory or exnref in this harness's build (legacy EH and relaxed SIMD came from the harness author's patches). Slower than wasm3 on every geomean row there (wasm3 1.01 vs WAMR 1.63 on M4).
caveats: Compared against a forked Wasmtime Pulley (v49.0.0 + 9 commits by the harness author), and WAMR main carries 29 harness patches, so neither side is a stock release. wasmi-benchmarks on AMD EPYC 7763 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) puts WAMR fast-interpreter execution at x17.07 vs Wasmtime (Pulley) x27.92 and Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1.15. Snippet only, not opened: a search snippet of Frank Denis's June 2026 libsodium post (00f.net, blocked here) says WAMR in AOT mode ran at 1.57x native vs Wasmtime 2.41x native, using wamrc --cpu=x86-64-v4 --opt-level=3, which may not be an equal-flags comparison. The AOT compiler, not the interpreter, is the part that competes with Wasmtime's JIT.
found_via: WebSearch 'github WebAssembly interpreter faster than wasm3 OR faster than wasmtime benchmark CoreMark C++ runtime' -> rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark (Pulley vs WAMR); WebSearch of 00f.net for the 2026 post

name: WAVM
baseline: Wasmer (LLVM, Cranelift and Singlepass backends), Wasmtime, V8 (Node.js)
workload: libsodium 1.0.18-stable built-in benchmark suite (crypto primitives and codecs) compiled to wasm32-wasi and run unchanged on every runtime.
claimed_speedup: 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test'; about 15% faster than wasmer's LLVM backend; V8 (nodejs) second. Per-test numbers are only in PNG charts.
compiler_and_flags: libsodium wasm32-wasi.sh --bench with system LLVM 11.1.0, wasm-opt -O4 on the output; runtimes built from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode (Node.js stock binary)
hardware: not stated (an unnamed macOS laptop for the main run; a separate unnamed Linux/x86_64 machine for the LLVM-runtime comparison)
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time LLVM compilation: slow to compile, large dependency on a specific LLVM version. Supports x86-64 and AArch64; the 2021 ARM run could not use WAVM because no prebuilt binary exists.
caveats: The data are from February 2021 and the README gives prose plus PNG charts, no numeric table. A search snippet of the author's June 2026 post (page blocked here) says Wasmer is now the best performer with WAVM, WAMR and Wasmtime close, so the 2021 lead may be gone. No hardware model is stated. wasmi-benchmarks does not include WAVM.
found_via: WebSearch 'WebAssembly runtime benchmark comparison wasmtime wasmer WAMR wasm3 WasmEdge results' -> 00f.net 2021 Q1 benchmark; opened the same text in the jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2021-Q1 README

name: Silverfir-nano
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter (execution) and Wasmtime Cranelift (startup)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks execution suite: 22 cases (counters, fibonacci, sort, nbody, argon2, json-parse, regex-redux and others), geometric mean of per-case ratios against the fastest runtime for each case.
claimed_speedup: Execution geomean on AMD EPYC 7763 relative to the per-case fastest runtime (lower is better): Silverfir-nano interpreter x9.02 versus WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, Wasm3 (eager) x16.51 and Wasmtime (Pulley) x27.92 (about 1.9x faster than WAMR, derived from page data); Silverfir-nano JIT x1.25, close to but not beating Wasmtime (Cranelift) x1.15, Wasmer (Cranelift) x1.17 and V8 x1.05; Wasmtime (Winch) is x2.35 and Wasmer (Singlepass) x2.95.
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks Cargo.toml: [profile.bench] lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1; Rust toolchain version not pinned in the repo and the C/C++ runtimes are built by their Rust wrapper crates under that profile (not verified)
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (named in the plot title; the plots repo also holds data for Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, an Intel i7700 and Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C, not read here)
tradeoffs: Ships both an interpreter and an on-device optimizing JIT; no_std; targets six ISAs from x86_64 and ARM64 down to RV32 and Thumb-2. Binary 337 KiB with the interpreter and 1,042 KiB with the JIT (README, RP2350 firmware).

name: wasmz
baseline: Wasmtime Pulley interpreter and WAMR fast interpreter
workload: Interpreter-only comparison of 7 runtimes on Apple Silicon E-cores: 17 shared cases, CPU time per call.
claimed_speedup: CPU time per call relative to the fastest runtime, geometric mean over 17 cases, N=10: Apple M4 Max E-cores wasmz 1.59 vs WAMR 1.63 and Pulley 2.09 (about 1.3x faster than Pulley, derived from page data); iPhone XS (A12) E-cores wasmz 1.63 vs Pulley 1.68 but WAMR 1.38.
compiler_and_flags: zig 0.16.0 -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (zig build static-lib), wasmz v0.1.4; Pulley built with Rust nightly-2026-07-05, fat LTO, --cfg=pulley_tail_calls; Apple clang 21.0.0
hardware: MacBook Pro Apple M4 Max (E-cores) and iPhone XS Max (Apple A12 Bionic, E-cores)
tradeoffs: Zig library with C API and Rust bindings; GC, SIMD, exceptions and threads claimed.
caveats: The same report lists wasmz failing six rows with wrong results, traps and crashes, getting extended-const and catch_ref/throw_ref wrong, having no multi-memory, and never collecting GC structs while an instance lives; the geomean covers only the 17 cases every runtime runs. The README's claim 'currently the fastest WebAssembly interpreter I have tested' is not what this independent run shows (wasm3 is 1.01). Forked Wasmtime Pulley baseline (v49.0.0 + 9 commits). On wasmi-benchmarks (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wasmi-labs/wasmi-benchmarks-plots/HEAD/data/amd-epyc-7763/lin-scale/geomean-execute.svg) wasmz is x15.89 vs WAMR fast-interpreter x17.07, behind Silverfir-nano x9.02 and Wasmi v2 x12.40.

name: wasm2c (WABT)
workload: libsodium WebAssembly benchmark built with the wide_arithmetic proposal, wasm2c output compiled by a C compiler vs running the same module in Wasmtime and Wasmer.
claimed_speedup: wasm2c used 0.887x as much time as Wasmer 7.1.0 and 0.814x as much as Wasmtime 46.0.0 on the geomean (snippet only).
tradeoffs: Ahead-of-time Wasm to portable C: no runtime, the module must be precompiled and the host supplies imports and libc support; wasm2c's runtime support for wide arithmetic uses compiler carry intrinsics and 128-bit integers.
caveats: Snippet only: 00f.net is blocked here (EGRESS_BLOCKED), the numbers come from a WebSearch summary of Frank Denis's 2026-07-08 post and were not read on the page; compiler, flags and CPU unknown.
